claim: Human volunteers learned novel association rules based on simple visual features in two fMRI experiments.
source: Here, in two fMRI experiments, we demonstrate a mechanism of abstraction built upon the valuation of sensory features. Human volunteers learned novel association rules based on simple visual features.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that human volunteers learned novel association rules based on simple visual features in two fMRI experiments.

claim: With learning, high-value abstract representations increasingly guided participant behaviour, resulting in better choices and higher subjective confidence.
source: Reinforcement-learning algorithms revealed that, with learning, high-value abstract representations increasingly guided participant behaviour, resulting in better choices and higher subjective confidence.
evidence: The abstract states that reinforcement-learning algorithms revealed this finding based on the experimental data.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) computes value signals.
source: We also found that the brain area computing value signals – the ventromedial prefrontal cortex – prioritised and selected latent task elements during abstraction, both locally and through its connection to the visual cortex.
evidence: The abstract explicitly identifies the vmPFC as the brain area computing value signals, supported by fMRI data.

claim: The vmPFC prioritised and selected latent task elements during abstraction, both locally and through its connection to the visual cortex.
source: We also found that the brain area computing value signals – the ventromedial prefrontal cortex – prioritised and selected latent task elements during abstraction, both locally and through its connection to the visual cortex.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on fMRI experimental data.

claim: Tagging the neural representation of a task feature with rewards evoked abstraction-based decisions.
source: Tagging the neural representation of a task feature with rewards evoked abstraction-based decisions.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from the second experiment using multivoxel neural reinforcement.

claim: Value is a goal-dependent, key factor in forging abstract representations.
source: Together, these findings provide a novel interpretation of value as a goal-dependent, key factor in forging abstract representations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Abstraction is the unique ability of the human mind to organise information beyond the immediate sensory reality.
source: Art is one of the best examples of abstraction, the unique ability of the human mind to organise information beyond the immediate sensory reality.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about abstraction presented in the introduction.

claim: Classic RL algorithms rapidly collapse in complex and/or multidimensional problems.
source: This is well exemplified in reinforcement learning (RL), where in complex and/or multidimensional problems, classic RL algorithms rapidly collapse (Bellman, 1957; Kawato and Samejima, 2007; Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in reinforcement learning.

claim: If an agent is able to first 'abstract' the current state to a lower dimensional manifold, representing only relevant features, behaviour becomes far more flexible and efficient.
source: If, on the other hand, the agent is able to first 'abstract' the current state to a lower dimensional manifold, representing only relevant features, behaviour becomes far more flexible and efficient (Ho et al., 2019; Konidaris, 2019; Niv, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Attention and the ability to act upon subspaces, concepts or abstract representations has been proposed as an effective solution to overcome computational bottlenecks arising from sensory-level operations in RL.
source: Attention (Farashahi et al., 2017; Leong et al., 2017; Niv et al., 2015), and more generally, the ability to act upon subspaces, concepts or abstract representations has been proposed as an effective solution to overcome computational bottlenecks arising from sensory-level operations in RL (Cortese et al., 2019; Hashemzadeh et al., 2019; Ho et al., 2019; Konidaris, 2019; Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Abstractions can be thought of as simplified maps carved from higher dimensional space, in which details have been removed or transformed, in order to focus on a subset of interconnected features.
source: Abstractions can be thus thought of as simplified maps carved from higher dimensional space, in which details have been removed or transformed, in order to focus on a subset of interconnected features, that is, a higher order concept, category or schema (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Mack et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conceptual definition supported by citations.

claim: For flexible deployment, abstraction should depend on task goals.
source: For flexible deployment, abstraction should depend on task goals.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on reasoning about abstraction.

claim: Task goals generally determine what is valuable.
source: From a psychological or neuroeconomic point of view, task goals generally determine what is valuable (Kobayashi and Hsu, 2019; Liu et al., 2017; McNamee et al., 2013), such that if one needs to light a fire, matches are much more valuable than a glass of water.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in psychology and neuroeconomics.

claim: Valuation processes are directly related to abstraction.
source: Hence, we hypothesised that valuation processes are directly related to abstraction.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: Value representations have been linked to neural activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) in the context of economic choices.
source: Value representations have been linked to neural activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) in the context of economic choices (McNamee et al., 2013; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The role of the vmPFC has been extended to computation of confidence.
source: More recently, the role of the vmPFC has also been extended to computation of confidence (De Martino et al., 2013; Gherman and Philiastides, 2018; Lebreton et al., 2015; Shapiro and Grafton, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: The vmPFC is crucial for formation of schemas or conceptual knowledge.
source: In the field of memory, a large corpus of work has shown that the vmPFC is crucial for formation of schemas or conceptual knowledge (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Kumaran et al., 2009; Mack et al., 2016; Tse et al., 2007), as well as generalisations (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work in memory research.

claim: The vmPFC collates goal-relevant information from elsewhere in the brain.
source: The vmPFC also collates goal-relevant information from elsewhere in the brain (Benoit et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The vmPFC is well suited to serve a pivotal function in the circuit that involves the hippocampal formation (HPC) and the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), dedicated to extracting latent task information and regularities important for navigating behavioural goals.
source: Considering its connectivity pattern (Neubert et al., 2015), the vmPFC is well suited to serve a pivotal function in the circuit that involves the hippocampal formation (HPC) and the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), dedicated to extracting latent task information and regularities important for navigating behavioural goals (Niv, 2019; Schuck et al., 2016; Stachenfeld et al., 2017; Viganò and Piazza, 2020; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on brain connectivity and function.

claim: Abstraction emerges during the course of learning.
source: Thus, the aim of this study is twofold: (i) to demonstrate that abstraction emerges during the course of learning, and (ii) to investigate how the brain, and specifically the vmPFC, uses valuation upon low-level sensory features to forge abstract representations.
evidence: This is one of the two main aims of the study, to be demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: The brain, and specifically the vmPFC, uses valuation upon low-level sensory features to forge abstract representations.
source: Thus, the aim of this study is twofold: (i) to demonstrate that abstraction emerges during the course of learning, and (ii) to investigate how the brain, and specifically the vmPFC, uses valuation upon low-level sensory features to forge abstract representations.
evidence: This is the second main aim of the study, to be investigated through experimental data.

claim: Participants' confidence in having performed the task well was positively correlated with their ability to abstract.
source: Participants' confidence in having performed the task well was positively correlated with their ability to abstract.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the introduction, referring to results shown in the paper.

claim: The vmPFC and its connection to the visual cortex construct abstract representations through a goal-dependent valuation process that is implemented as top-down control of sensory cortices.
source: To anticipate our results, we show that the vmPFC and its connection to the visual cortex construct abstract representations through a goal-dependent valuation process that is implemented as top-down control of sensory cortices.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings presented in the introduction.

claim: Participants (N = 33) learned the fruit preference of pacman-like characters formed by the combination of three visual features (colour, mouth direction, and stripe orientation).
source: Participants (N = 33) learned the fruit preference of pacman-like characters formed by the combination of three visual features (colour, mouth direction, and stripe orientation, Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by Figure 1A-B.

claim: The preference was governed by a combination of two features, selected randomly by the computer program for each block.
source: The preference was governed by a combination of two features, selected randomly by our computer program for each block (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by Figure 1A-B.

claim: Participants were instructed that one feature was irrelevant, but they did not know which.
source: Although participants were instructed that one feature was irrelevant, they did not know which.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Within blocks, performance was higher than chance as early as the second trial.
source: Within blocks, performance was higher than chance as early as the second trial (Figure 1C, one-sample t-test against mean of 0.5, trial 2: t32 = 4.13, P(FDR) < 10−3, trial 3: t32 = 2.47, P(FDR) = 0.014, all trials t>3: P(FDR) < 10−3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Learning speed increased significantly across blocks.
source: Considering the whole experimental session, learning speed (i.e. how quickly participants completed a given block) increased significantly across blocks (Figure 1D, N = 11 time points, Pearson's r = 0.80, p = 0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Participants' self-reports of confidence correlated with their learning speed.
source: When at the end of a session, participants were asked about their degree of confidence in having performed the task well, their self-reports correlated with their learning speed (N = 31 [2 missing data], robust regression slope = 0.024, t29 = 3.27, p = 0.003, Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, supported by Figure 1E.

claim: Participants' confidence did not correlate with the overall number of trials or the product of the proportion of successes.
source: but not with the overall number of trials, or the product of the proportion of successes (learning speed: Pearson's r = 0.53, p = 0.002, total trials: r = −0.13, p = 0.47, test for difference in r: z = 2.71, p = 0.007; product of the proportion of successes: r = −0.06, p = 0.75, test for difference in r: z = 2.43, p = 0.015).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data.

claim: The block type or association type did not systematically affect learning speed.
source: We also confirmed that the block type (defined by relevant features, e.g., colour-orientation) or association type (e.g. symmetric 2x2) did not systematically affect learning speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Excluded participants had overall lower performance.
source: Excluded participants (see Materials and methods) had overall lower performance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), although some had comparable ratios correct.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Feature RL explicitly tracked all combinations of three features, 2^3 = eight states.
source: The first algorithm, called Feature RL, explicitly tracked all combinations of three features, 23 = eight states (Figure 2A, top left).
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Abstract RL used a more compact or abstract state representation in which only two features are tracked, 2^2 = four states.
source: Conversely, the second algorithm, called Abstract RL, used a more compact or abstract state representation in which only two features are tracked. These compressed representations reduce the explored state-space by half, 22 = four states (Figure 2A, top right).
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: As many as three Abstract RL in parallel were possible, one for each combination of two features.
source: Importantly, in this task environment as many as three Abstract RL in parallel were possible, one for each combination of two features.
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.

claim: Simulations indicated that expected value and responsibility were highest for the appropriate Abstract RL, followed by Feature RL, and the two Abstract RLs based on irrelevant features as the lowest.
source: Simulations indicated that expected value and responsibility were highest for the appropriate Abstract RL, followed by Feature RL, and the two Abstract RLs based on irrelevant features as the lowest (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations, supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Participant empirical data displayed the same pattern as simulations, whereby the value function and responsibility signal of the appropriate Abstract RL were higher than in other RL algorithms.
source: Participant empirical data displayed the same pattern, whereby the value function and responsibility signal of the appropriate Abstract RL were higher than in other RL algorithms (Figure 2D, right side).
evidence: This is a finding from participant data, supported by Figure 2D.

claim: The RPE variance was associated with participant learning speed, such that participants who learned block rules quickly were sharper in expert selection.
source: Crucially, the variance v was associated with participant learning speed, such that participants who learned block rules quickly were sharper in expert selection (Figure 2E, N = 29, robust regression slope = −1.02, t27 = −2.59, p = 0.015).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the modeling analysis, supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Feature RL was slower and less efficient than Abstract RL in simulations.
source: The simulations attested that Feature RL was slower and less efficient (Figure 3A), yielding lower learning speed and a higher percentage of failed blocks.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Where learning proceeded slowly, Feature RL was consistently predominant, while the reverse happened in blocks where participants displayed fast learning.
source: Where learning proceeded slowly, Feature RL was consistently predominant (Figure 3B), while the reverse happened in blocks where participants displayed fast learning (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from participant data, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Among participants, the degree of abstraction (propensity to use Abstract RL) correlated with the empirical learning speed.
source: Among participants, the degree of abstraction (propensity to use Abstract RL) correlated with the empirical learning speed (N = 33, robust regression, slope = 0.52, t31 = 4.56, p = 7.64x10−5, Figure 3C top).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from participant data, supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Participant confidence in having performed the task well was significantly correlated with the degree of abstraction.
source: Participant confidence in having performed the task well was also significantly correlated with the degree of abstraction (N = 31, robust regression, slope = 0.026, t29 = 2.69, p = 0.012, Figure 3C, bottom).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from participant data, supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Feature RL appeared to have higher learning rates α compared with Abstract RL when considering all blocks regardless of fit.
source: Considering all blocks regardless of fit (paired comparison), feature RL appeared to have higher learning rates α compared with Abstract RL (two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test against median 0, z = 14.33, p < 10−30, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the modeling analysis, supported by Figure 3D.

claim: A similar asymmetry was found with greediness between Feature RL and Abstract RL.
source: A similar asymmetry was found with greediness (Figure 3E, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test against median 0, z = 7.14, p < 10−10).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the modeling analysis, supported by Figure 3E.

claim: On their first block, most participants relied on Feature RL, while the pattern reversed in the last block.
source: On their first block, most participants relied on Feature RL, while the pattern reversed in the last block (two-sided sign test, z = −2.77, p = 0.006, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from participant data, supported by Figure 3F.

claim: Computing the abstraction level separately for the session median split of early and late blocks resulted in higher abstraction in late blocks.
source: Computing the abstraction level separately for the session median split of early and late blocks also resulted in higher abstraction in late blocks (two-sided sign test, z = −2.94, p = 0.003, Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from participant data, supported by Figure 3G.

claim: Activity in the vmPFC strongly correlated with value magnitude at stimulus presentation time.
source: As predicted, activity in the vmPFC strongly correlated with value magnitude (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI data analysis, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Activity in insular and dorsal prefrontal cortices increased under conditions of low expected value.
source: Concurrently, activity in insular and dorsal prefrontal cortices increased under conditions of low expected value. This pattern of activity is consistent with previous studies on error monitoring and processing (Bastin et al., 2017; Carter et al., 1998; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI data analysis, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior work.

claim: Only connectivity between the visual cortex (VC) and vmPFC was higher on trials that carried large expected value, compared to low-value trials.
source: Supporting the idea that the vmPFC based its predictions on the integration of visual features, only connectivity between the visual cortex (VC) and vmPFC was higher on trials that carried large expected value, compared to low-value trials (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from PPI analysis of fMRI data, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: The strength of the VC - vmPFC interaction was associated with the overall learning speed among participants.
source: Strikingly, the strength of this VC - vmPFC interaction was associated with the overall learning speed among participants (N = 31, robust regression, slope = 0.016, t29 = 2.55, p = 0.016, Figure 4C), such that participants with stronger modulation of the coupling between the vmPFC and VC also learned block rules faster.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from fMRI and behavioral data, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: vmPFC activity levels distinguished Feature RL and Abstract RL cases well.
source: Post-hoc comparisons showed vmPFC activity levels distinguished Feature RL and Abstract RL cases well (LMEM: t64 = 2.94, p(FDR) = 0.009), while the HPC remained agnostic to the style of learning (LMEM: t64 = 0.62, p(FDR) = 0.54).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from fMRI data analysis.

claim: The HPC remained agnostic to the style of learning (Feature RL vs Abstract RL).
source: Post-hoc comparisons showed vmPFC activity levels distinguished Feature RL and Abstract RL cases well (LMEM: t64 = 2.94, p(FDR) = 0.009), while the HPC remained agnostic to the style of learning (LMEM: t64 = 0.62, p(FDR) = 0.54).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from fMRI data analysis.

claim: Classification accuracy was significantly higher in Abstract RL trials compared with Feature RL trials in both the HPC and vmPFC.
source: We found that classification accuracy was significantly higher in Abstract RL trials compared with Feature RL trials in both the HPC and vmPFC (two-sided t-test, HPC: t32 = −2.37, p(FDR) < 0.036, vmPFC: t32 = −2.51, p(FDR) = 0.036, Figure 5C)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from MVPA of fMRI data, supported by Figure 5C.

claim: The difference in feature decodability was of opposite sign in VC compared to HPC and vmPFC.
source: while the difference was of opposite sign in VC (t32 = 1.61, p(FDR) = 0.12, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from MVPA of fMRI data, supported by Figure 5C.

claim: The increased feature decodability in Abstract RL was significantly larger in the HPC and vmPFC compared to the VC.
source: The increased feature decodability in Abstract RL was significantly larger in the HPC and vmPFC compared to the VC (LMEM model 'y ~ ROI + (1|participants)', y: difference in decodability, t97 = 3.37, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from MVPA of fMRI data.

claim: Significant reduction in decoding accuracy was detected in the OFC, ACC, vmPFC and dorsolateral PFC when a feature was irrelevant to the rule, compared to when it was relevant.
source: Beside the occipital cortex, significant reduction in decoding accuracy was also detected in the OFC, ACC, vmPFC and dorsolateral PFC when a feature was irrelevant to the rule, compared to when it was relevant (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from searchlight MVPA of fMRI data, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: Artificially adding value to a neural representation of a target task-related feature in VC resulted in increased use of abstractions.
source: We used this procedure in a follow-up experiment (N = 22, a subgroup from the main experiment; see Materials and methods) to artificially add value (rewards) to neural representation in VC of a target task-related feature (Figure 6A). At the end of two training sessions, participants completed 16 blocks of the pacman fruit preference task, outside of the scanner. Task blocks could be labelled as 'relevant' (eight blocks) if the feature tagged with value was relevant to the block rule, or 'irrelevant' otherwise (eight blocks).
evidence: This describes the neurofeedback experiment design and its results, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: 'Relevant' blocks appeared to be associated with a behavioural shift toward Abstract RL, whereas there was no substantial qualitative effect in 'irrelevant' blocks.
source: 'Relevant' blocks appeared to be associated with a behavioural shift toward Abstract RL, whereas there was no substantial qualitative effect in 'irrelevant' blocks (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the neurofeedback experiment, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Behaviour in blocks where the targeted feature was relevant displayed markedly increased abstraction.
source: To quantify this effect, we first applied a binomial test, finding that behaviour in blocks where the targeted feature was relevant displayed markedly increased abstraction (base rate 0.5, number of Abstract RL blocks given total number of blocks; 'relevant': P(123|176) = 1.37x10−7, 'irrelevant': P(90|176) = 0.82).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the neurofeedback experiment.

claim: Participants increased their use of abstraction in 'relevant' blocks, whereas no significant difference was detected in the 'irrelevant' blocks.
source: Participants increased their use of abstraction in 'relevant' blocks, whereas no significant difference was detected in the 'irrelevant' blocks (Figure 6C, two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test, 'relevant' blocks: z = 2.44, p = 0.015, 'irrelevant' blocks: z = −1.55, p = 0.12, 'relevant' vs 'irrelevant': z = 4.01, p = 6.03x10−5).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the neurofeedback experiment, supported by Figure 6C.

claim: Behaviour in 'relevant' blocks was more likely to be driven by Abstract RL.
source: Replicating the results reported above, behaviour in 'relevant' blocks was more likely to be driven by Abstract RL (Figure 6D, perm. test p < 0.001), while Feature RL tended to appear more in 'irrelevant' blocks.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the neurofeedback experiment, supported by Figure 6D.

claim: Participants who were more successful at neurofeedback were more likely to display larger increases in abstraction in the subsequent behavioural test compared to their initial level.
source: Furthermore, those who were more successful were also more likely to display larger increases in abstraction in the subsequent behavioural test compared to their initial level (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the neurofeedback experiment, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Participants explored and used task dimensionality through learning, as they shifted from a simple feature-based strategy to using more sophisticated abstractions.
source: Participants explored and used task dimensionality through learning, as they shifted from a simple feature-based strategy to using more sophisticated abstractions.
evidence: This is a main finding from the study, supported by the behavioral and modeling results.

claim: The more participants used Abstract RL, the faster they became at solving the task.
source: The more participants used Abstract RL, the faster they became at solving the task.
evidence: This is a main finding from the study, supported by the behavioral and modeling results.

claim: In this task, to learn faster, an agent must use Abstract RL, as other strategies would result in slower completion of task blocks.
source: Note that in this task, structure, learning speed, and abstraction are linked. To learn faster, an agent must use Abstract RL, as other strategies would result in slower completion of task blocks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the task design and modeling results.

claim: Efficient decision-making processes in the brain depend on higher-order, summarised representations of task-states.
source: These results build on the idea that efficient decision-making processes in the brain depend on higher-order, summarised representations of task-states (Niv, 2019; Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Abstraction likely requires a functional link between sensory regions and areas encoding value predictions about task states.
source: Further, abstraction likely requires a functional link between sensory regions and areas encoding value predictions about task states (Figure 4C, the VC-vmPFC coupling was positively correlated with participant's learning speed).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PPI analysis results, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Estimating reward value of individual features provides a reliable and adaptive mechanism in RL.
source: This is consistent with previous work that demonstrates how estimating reward value of individual features provides a reliable and adaptive mechanism in RL (Farashahi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mechanism of feature valuation may support formation of abstract representations to be further used for learning computations, for example selection of the appropriate abstract representation.
source: We extend this notion by showing that the mechanism may support formation of abstract representations to be further used for learning computations, for example selection of the appropriate abstract representation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The role of the HPC is to store, index, and update conceptual/schematic memories.
source: Likely, the role of the HPC is to store, index, and update conceptual/schematic memories (Mack et al., 2016; Tse et al., 2011; Tse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 'Creation' of new concepts or schemas may occur in the mPFC or the vmPFC in humans.
source: 'Creation' of new concepts or schemas may occur elsewhere. A good candidate could be the mPFC or the vmPFC in humans (Mack et al., 2020; Tse et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The vmPFC exhibits value signals directly modulated by cognitive requirements.
source: Indeed, the vmPFC exhibits value signals directly modulated by cognitive requirements (Castegnetti et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: vmPFC-driven valuation of low-level sensory information serves to channel-specific features/components to higher order areas.
source: Our results expose a potential mechanism of how the vmPFC interacts with the HPC in construction of goal-relevant abstractions. vmPFC-driven valuation of low-level sensory information serves to channel-specific features/components to higher order areas (e.g. the HPC, vmPFC, but also the dorsal prefrontal cortex, for instance).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The vmPFC was more engaged in Abstract RL, while the HPC was equally active under both abstract and feature-based strategies.
source: Congruent with this interpretation, we found that the vmPFC was more engaged in Abstract RL, while the HPC was equally active under both abstract and feature-based strategies (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI data analysis, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: When a feature was irrelevant to the rule, its decodability from activity patterns in OFC/DLPFC decreased.
source: When a feature was irrelevant to the rule, its decodability from activity patterns in OFC/DLPFC decreased (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from MVPA of fMRI data, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: Prefrontal regions play a role in constructing goal-dependent task states and abstract rules from relevant sensory information.
source: These findings accord well with the role of prefrontal regions in constructing goal-dependent task states and abstract rules from relevant sensory information (Akaishi et al., 2016; Schuck et al., 2016; Wallis et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Block rules were encoded in multivoxel activity patterns within the OFC/DLPFC circuitry.
source: Furthermore, we found block rules were also encoded in multivoxel activity patterns within the OFC/DLPFC circuitry (Figure 5E; Bengtsson et al., 2009; Mian et al., 2014; Wallis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from MVPA of fMRI data, supported by Figure 5E and citations to prior work.

claim: There is no single region of the brain that maintains a fixed task state; rather, the configuration of elements that determines a state is continuously reconstructed over time.
source: This study nevertheless suggests that there is no single region of the brain that maintains a fixed task state. Rather, the configuration of elements that determines a state is continuously reconstructed over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: By continuously recomputing task states, the agent can make more robust decisions because these are related to the subset of most relevant, up-to-date information.
source: By continuously recomputing task states, the agent can make more robust decisions because these are related to the subset of most relevant, up-to-date information.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference based on the study's findings.

claim: HPC neurons continuously generate representations of alternative future trajectories.
source: Such a computational coding scheme shares strong analogies with HPC neural coding, whereby neurons continuously generate representations of alternative future trajectories (Kay et al., 2020), and replay past cognitive trajectories (Schuck and Niv, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HPC neurons replay past cognitive trajectories.
source: Such a computational coding scheme shares strong analogies with HPC neural coding, whereby neurons continuously generate representations of alternative future trajectories (Kay et al., 2020), and replay past cognitive trajectories (Schuck and Niv, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The study leveraged simple visual features (colour, or stripe orientation), rather than more complex stimuli or objects that can be linked conceptually.
source: One significant topic for discussion concerns the elements used to construct abstractions. We leveraged simple visual features (colour, or stripe orientation), rather than more complex stimuli or objects that can be linked conceptually (Kumaran et al., 2009; Zeithamova et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental design choice.

claim: The study effectively studied one of the lowest levels of abstraction.
source: In this work, we effectively studied one of the lowest levels of abstraction.
evidence: This is a characterization of the study's scope.

claim: It is unlikely that the brain uses an entirely different strategy to generate new representations at different levels of abstraction.
source: While our work cannot decisively support this, we believe it unlikely that the brain uses an entirely different strategy to generate new representations at different levels of abstraction.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the study's findings.

claim: The internal source of information abstracted should be different at different levels of abstraction, but the algorithm itself should be the same or highly similar.
source: Rather, the internal source of information abstracted should be different, but the algorithm itself should be the same or, at the very least, highly similar.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the study's findings.

claim: Learning through abstraction of simple visual features should be related to early VC.
source: The fact our PPI analysis showed a link between the vmPFC and VC may point to this distinguishing characteristic of our study. Learning through abstraction of simple visual features should be related to early VC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PPI analysis results.

claim: Features in other modalities, for example, auditory, would involve functional coupling between the auditory cortex and the vmPFC.
source: Features in other modalities, for example, auditory, would involve functional coupling between the auditory cortex and the vmPFC.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the study's findings.

claim: When learning about more complex objects or categories, we expect to see stronger reliance on the HPC.
source: When learning about more complex objects or categories, we expect to see stronger reliance on the HPC (Kumaran et al., 2009; Mack et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the study's findings and citations to prior work.

claim: Depending on which type of information is relevant at any point in time, different areas will be coupled with the vmPFC to generate value representations.
source: Depending on which type of information is relevant at any point in time, we suspect that different areas will be coupled with the vmPFC to generate value representations.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the study's findings.

claim: The facilitating effect of value on abstraction can be directly linked to changes in the early processing stage of visual information.
source: Artificially adding value in the form of reward to a feature representation in the VC resulted in increased use of abstractions. Thus, the facilitating effect of value on abstraction can be directly linked to changes in the early processing stage of visual information.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurofeedback experiment results.

claim: Value governs a functional remapping in the sensory cortex by direct lateral OFC projections carrying RPE information.
source: Consonant with this interpretation, recent work in mice has elegantly reported how value governs a functional remapping in the sensory cortex by direct lateral OFC projections carrying RPE information (Banerjee et al., 2020), as well as by modulating the gain of neurons to irrelevant stimuli (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work in mice.

claim: Value modulates the gain of neurons to irrelevant stimuli in the sensory cortex.
source: Consonant with this interpretation, recent work in mice has elegantly reported how value governs a functional remapping in the sensory cortex by direct lateral OFC projections carrying RPE information (Banerjee et al., 2020), as well as by modulating the gain of neurons to irrelevant stimuli (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work in mice.

claim: It remains to be investigated whether the effect of value results in more efficient construction of abstract representations, or in better selection of internal abstract models.
source: While these considerations clearly point to a central role of the vmPFC and valuation in abstraction by controlling sensory representations, it remains to be investigated whether this effect results in more efficient construction of abstract representations, or in better selection of internal abstract models.
evidence: This identifies an open question for future research.

claim: Parallel circuits linking the prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia could track different levels of abstraction, possibly in hierarchical fashion.
source: We speculate that parallel circuits linking the prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia could track these levels of abstraction, possibly in hierarchical fashion (Badre and Frank, 2012; Cortese et al., 2019; Haruno and Kawato, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to prior work.

claim: If top-down attention were the sole driver in Abstract RL, we would expect to see a marked increase in feature decodability in VC.
source: Yet, if top-down attention were the sole driver in Abstract RL, we contend that the pattern of results would have been different. For example, we would expect to see a marked increase in feature decodability in VC (Guggenmos et al., 2015; Kamitani and Tong, 2005).
evidence: This is a counterfactual argument supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Decoded neurofeedback operates unconsciously.
source: Because decoded neurofeedback operates unconsciously (Muñoz-Moldes and Cleeremans, 2020; Shibata et al., 2019), value was added directly at the sensory representation level (limited to the targeted region), precluding alternative top-down effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on decoded neurofeedback.

claim: Attention is most likely an effector of the abstraction and valuation processes.
source: That is not to say that attention does not significantly mediate this type of abstract learning; however, we argue that attention is most likely an effector of the abstraction and valuation processes (Krauzlis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The degree of neural compression in the vmPFC has been shown to relate to features most predictive of positive outcomes, under a given goal.
source: The degree of neural compression in the vmPFC has been shown to relate to features most predictive of positive outcomes, under a given goal (Mack et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neural activity in the PFC (and HPC) explicitly generates representations that are simultaneously abstract and high dimensional.
source: Similarly, the geometry of neural activity in generalisation may be key here. Neural activity in the PFC (and HPC) explicitly generates representations that are simultaneously abstract and high dimensional (Bernardi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Valuation may be interpreted as an abstraction in itself, providing a simple and efficient way for the brain to operate on a dimensionless axis.
source: An attractive view is that valuation may be interpreted as an abstraction in itself. Value could provide a simple and efficient way for the brain to operate on a dimensionless axis.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Each point on the value axis could index a certain task state, or even behavioural strategy, as a function of its assigned abstract value.
source: Each point on this axis could index a certain task state, or even behavioural strategy, as a function of its assigned abstract value.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Neuronal encoding of feature-specific value, or choice options, may help the system construct useful representations that can inform flexible behavioural strategies.
source: Neuronal encoding of feature-specific value, or choice options, may help the system construct useful representations that can, in turn, inform flexible behavioural strategies (Niv, 2019; Schuck et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Valuation subserves a critical function in constructing abstractions.
source: In summary, this work provides evidence for a function of valuation that exceeds the classic view in decision-making and neuroeconomics. We show that valuation subserves a critical function in constructing abstractions.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Valuation, by generating a common currency across perceptually different stimuli, may be an abstraction in itself, and is tightly linked to the concept of task states in decision-making.
source: One may further speculate that valuation, by generating a common currency across perceptually different stimuli, may be an abstraction in itself, and that it is tightly linked to the concept of task states in decision-making.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: This work reconciles apparently disconnected findings in decision-making and memory literature on the role of the vmPFC.
source: We believe this work not only offers a new perspective on the role of valuation in generating abstract thoughts, but also reconciles apparently disconnected findings in decision-making and memory literature on the role of the vmPFC.
evidence: This is a claim about the broader significance of the study.

claim: Value is not a simple proxy of a numerical reward signal, but is better understood as a conceptual representation or schema built on-the-fly to respond to a specific behavioural demand.
source: In this context, value is not a simple proxy of a numerical reward signal, but is better understood as a conceptual representation or schema built on-the-fly to respond to a specific behavioural demand.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Value signals in the brain play an important algorithmic role in development of sophisticated learning strategies.
source: Thus, we believe our findings provide a fresh view of the invariable presence of value signals in the brain that play an important algorithmic role in development of sophisticated learning strategies.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.
